scope: Motivating problem in PRS hypothesis testing.
span: For PRS analyses, which typically test for association between PRS and a trait(s) or outcome of interest, overlapping samples between the GWAS and target data samples can result in spurious inflation of the coefficient of determination (R2) and association P values, leading to false-positive and exaggerated findings [15].

conclusion: EraSOR inherits LD score regression assumptions, including similar genetic and environmental stratification between cohorts, whose violation can bias its estimates.
scope: Validation is limited to UK Biobank; authors advise against F_ST within or between cohorts above approximately 0.02 and recommend closely ancestry-matched single-ancestry data.
span: Our algorithm is not without limitation. First, as EraSOR relies on LD score intercept estimates for adjustment, all assumptions of LD score regression also apply to EraSOR. For instance, if the level of genetic and environmental stratification differs between the 2 cohorts, the bivariate LD score equation may not hold [13], which can lead to bias in EraSOR estimates.

assumptions: Tested UK Biobank simulations with European-ancestry base and target samples and the investigated trait and ascertainment scenarios.
conclusion: In the tested simulations, EraSOR almost entirely eliminated inflation from intercohort overlap and relatedness.
scope: Empirical performance statement restricted to tested simulations; not a general mathematical guarantee.
span: We observed that for both quantitative and binary traits, EraSOR almost entirely eliminates the inflation caused by intercohort overlap and relatedness in our simulations based on UK Biobank (European ancestry base and target samples) data (Fig. 2). These simulations modeled a range of scenarios that varied trait heritability, prevalence, degree of overlap, and combinations of overlap among cases and controls.

conclusion: The authors advise against EraSOR when the base GWAS has estimated SNP heritability below 5%.
scope: Low-heritability restriction; the derivation divides by heritability estimates.
span: EraSOR should not be applied to data on traits for which there is little evidence of heritability, since PRS analyses performed on underpowered GWAS are more likely to generate misleading results and conclusions based on them. Therefore, as for PRS analyses in general [1], we do not recommend the application of EraSOR to base GWAS data with estimated h2SNP <5%.

conclusion: EraSOR was tested with C+T and lassosum and inherits their limitations, including potential overfitting of PRS-trait associations.
scope: The authors expect similar qualitative behavior with other PRS methods but do not establish it.
span: Additionally, EraSOR has only been tested using the C+T and lassosum PRS calculation method and so is subject to their limitations, such as potential overfitting of PRS–trait associations. However, given the similar performance of different PRS methods [29], we do not expect qualitatively different results to those observed here when EraSOR is applied to correct for sample overlap in PRS analyses using other PRS methods.

objects: base and target cohort sizes; complete overlap
assumptions: Reliance on estimated LD score regression quantities.
conclusion: The authors state that both cohorts must exceed 1,000 samples for sufficiently accurate adjustment and 5,000 for consistent accuracy, and that complete overlap of equal-sized cohorts can leave residual inflation.
scope: Stated operating limits, not tunable thresholds; failure under complete overlap remains possible.
span: It is important to note that, due to reliance on LD score regression estimates, EraSOR only produces sufficiently accurate adjustments for application when both base and target cohorts have sample sizes greater than 1,000 and is only consistently accurate when both cohorts have greater than 5,000 samples. In addition, when there is a complete overlap between 2 equal-sized cohort, EraSOR can fail to fully adjust for the inflation caused by sample overlap.

objects: adjusted PRS-trait association; null-SNP overlap equations
assumptions: Application where SNPs truly contribute to the phenotype.
conclusion: EraSOR tends to underestimate PRS-trait associations, with misclassification of true signal by null-based overlap equations offered as a possible explanation.
scope: Author-stated tendency and proposed explanation; no proven bias bound or corrected equation.
span: In general, EraSOR tends to overcorrect, meaning that PRS–trait associations are underestimated after EraSOR adjustment. One possible explanation is that the equations by LeBlanc et al. [17] were based on the null model of no contribution of SNP to the trait. Thus, in cases where SNPs contribute to the phenotype of interest, there will be an upper bound to the level of inflation caused by sample overlap, and EraSOR might misclassify some of the true signal as inflation caused by sample overlap, leading to overcorrection of test statistics.
